scenarios.title: Building Your Study Plan
scenarios.situation: You have 6 weeks until your Blockchain Developer assessment. You work full-time and have 2 hours per evening plus weekends. You've tried studying before but kept losing momentum after week 2.
scenarios.prompt: What's the most effective study approach for sustained 6-week preparation?
choices: Follow the bootcamp's guided path in order: 2 hours daily mixing lessons, scenarios, and labs, with weekly review of weak areas and a full mock in week 5
Study 6 hours every Saturday and skip weekdays — cramming on weekends is more efficient
Read all lessons first (weeks 1-4), then do all scenarios (week 5), then labs (week 6)
Focus only on practice exams — studying content is less important than test familiarity
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Spaced, interleaved practice across 6 weeks builds durable knowledge. The guided path sequences foundations before advanced topics. Mixing lessons (input), scenarios (application), and labs (hands-on) every session engages all learning modes. Weekend-only cramming leads to burnout and poor retention. Reading everything before practicing means you forget early material.
scenarios.hint: Think about what the learning science says: spacing, interleaving, and active practice beat massed passive reading.
objectives: Design an effective multi-week study plan
Balance input, application, and hands-on practice
evidence: Spaced repetition improves long-term retention by 200%+ vs. massed practice (Cepeda et al.)

scenarios.title: Identifying Weak Areas
scenarios.situation: After 3 weeks of study, your scenario scores are: Networking 90%, Security 85%, Storage 60%, Troubleshooting 55%. The exam is in 3 weeks.
scenarios.prompt: How should you allocate your remaining study time?
choices: Shift 70% of study time to Storage and Troubleshooting (weakest areas) while maintaining Networking and Security with brief reviews
Continue studying all areas equally — balanced preparation is safest
Focus exclusively on Troubleshooting (lowest score) until it reaches 80%, then move on
Study only your strong areas to guarantee those points — weak areas are harder to improve
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Targeted remediation on weak areas yields the highest score improvement per hour. Your strong areas (90%, 85%) need only maintenance to prevent decay. Equal allocation wastes time on already-mastered content. Single-area focus risks neglecting Storage while over-investing in one domain.
scenarios.hint: Where is the most room for improvement? Which areas need maintenance vs. intensive work?
objectives: Analyze performance data to identify gaps
Prioritize study time for maximum score impact

scenarios.title: Exam Day Strategy
scenarios.situation: It's exam day. You have 90 minutes for 65 questions including performance-based simulations. You feel nervous.
scenarios.prompt: What's the best time management strategy?
choices: Quick first pass: answer confident questions immediately, flag uncertain ones, do performance-based last, then return to flagged items with remaining time
Answer every question in order, spending as much time as needed to be certain before moving on
Start with performance-based questions while your mind is fresh, then do multiple choice
Rush through all questions in 45 minutes, then use remaining time to double-check everything
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The two-pass method ensures you bank all confident points first, then allocate remaining time to harder questions. Performance-based questions are time-intensive — doing them last prevents getting stuck early. Answering in strict order risks running out of time on difficult items while easy points remain unclaimed.
scenarios.hint: Think about maximizing points per minute. Which questions give the best return on time invested?
objectives: Prioritize questions by confidence and time cost
evidence: 90 minutes | 65 questions | Mix of MCQ and performance-based

scenarios.title: When Reading Isn't Enough
scenarios.situation: You've read all the lessons twice and score 95% on knowledge checks, but only 60% on scenario questions and struggle with labs.
scenarios.prompt: What's the gap and how do you fix it?
choices: Knowledge without application: shift to scenarios and labs — narrate your reasoning aloud, redo failed labs until fluent, and practice explaining the 'why' behind each answer
Read the lessons a third time more carefully — you must have missed details
The scenarios are poorly written — focus on memorizing more facts instead
Take a break from studying — you're overthinking the practical questions
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. High knowledge-check scores with low scenario scores indicate a transfer gap — you know facts but can't apply them. Scenarios require connecting concepts to situations. Labs require procedural fluency. The fix is deliberate application practice: think aloud through scenarios, repeat labs until commands are automatic, and always ask 'why is this the best answer?' not just 'what is the answer?'
scenarios.hint: What's different between a knowledge check (recall) and a scenario (application)? Which skill needs practice?
objectives: Apply deliberate practice to build transfer

choices: It's just a slow database
A distributed ledger: an append-only, cryptographically-linked record replicated across participants, where consensus replaces the trusted intermediary
It's encryption for databases
It's only for cryptocurrency
scenarios.hint: What problem does the chain solve that a shared database doesn't — and what does it cost?
scenarios.prompt: What is a blockchain, fundamentally?
scenarios.situation: A stakeholder asks why the project needs a blockchain instead of a database.
scenarios.title: Why a chain?
scenarios.why: A blockchain is a trust technology, not a database technology: multiple mutually-distrusting parties agree on shared state without a central authority, via consensus and cryptographic linkage. That buys censorship resistance and auditability at the cost of throughput and complexity. If all parties trust one operator, a database wins — the chain's value is precisely where trust is absent.

choices: To make transactions fast
To let mutually distrusting participants agree on a single shared state without a central authority
To encrypt data
To reduce storage costs
scenarios.hint: What would happen if two participants disagreed about the ledger — and who resolves it?
scenarios.prompt: What problem does consensus solve?
scenarios.situation: You're explaining consensus to a backend engineer.
scenarios.title: Agreeing without a boss
scenarios.why: Consensus is the mechanism by which decentralized participants converge on one ledger state — ordering transactions and resolving conflicts without a trusted coordinator. Without it, every participant has their own version of truth and double-spending is trivial. Different mechanisms (PoW, PoS, XRPL consensus) make different trade-offs, but the problem they solve is identical: agreement among adversaries.

choices: They're the same thing
Permissionless: anyone can participate, security from economics/cryptography. Permissioned: known identified participants, access controlled — different trust assumptions, different fits
Permissioned is always more secure
Permissionless is always better
scenarios.hint: Who are you defending against in each model — anonymous attackers, or known-but-curious partners?
scenarios.prompt: When is each model appropriate?
scenarios.situation: An enterprise consortium debates public vs permissioned for inter-bank settlement.
scenarios.title: Choosing the model
scenarios.why: The models encode different trust assumptions: permissionless assumes adversarial anonymity (secured by economic incentives), permissioned assumes known identities with contractual/legal accountability. Inter-bank settlement among regulated entities fits permissioned — identity, privacy, and governance matter more than censorship resistance. The wrong model choice is the most expensive architectural mistake in the space.

choices: Finality means a transaction can never be reversed under the protocol's guarantees — probabilistic (PoW confirmations) vs deterministic (BFT-style) finality
Finality means the transaction is fast
All chains have the same finality
Finality doesn't matter for applications
scenarios.hint: After one Bitcoin confirmation, how sure are you — and after six?
scenarios.prompt: What is finality, and why do the models differ?
scenarios.situation: Your app must decide when a deposit is 'safe' to credit.
scenarios.title: When is it final?
scenarios.why: Finality is the guarantee a transaction won't be reversed: Bitcoin offers probabilistic finality (each confirmation exponentially reduces reversal odds — hence the 6-confirmation convention for large value), while BFT-style systems offer deterministic finality at ledger close. Your crediting policy must match the chain's finality model — crediting instantly on a PoW chain is how exchanges get double-spent.

choices: Blockchain fixes everything
When multiple distrusting parties need shared, tamper-evident state without a trusted intermediary — and not when one party is trusted, throughput matters most, or data must be deletable
Whenever there's a database
For all financial software
scenarios.hint: What does the chain give you that nothing else does — and what does it cost you?
scenarios.prompt: When should you NOT use a blockchain?
scenarios.situation: A team proposes blockchain for an internal single-company inventory system.
scenarios.title: The wrong tool
scenarios.why: Blockchain's benefits (trust minimization, tamper-evidence across distrusting parties) come at real costs: throughput limits, complexity, immutability conflicts with data-deletion requirements. A single trusted company running inventory gets all cost and no benefit — a database with audit logs is the honest answer. Saying 'no' to blockchain is often the most senior engineering call.

choices: Decentralization means no one is in charge of anything
A spectrum: distribution of control across participants, varying by layer (mining/validation, development, governance) — assess each layer, not the label
It's just marketing
Only node count matters
scenarios.hint: A chain with 10,000 nodes but 2 mining pools — how decentralized is it, really?
scenarios.prompt: How should engineers evaluate decentralization claims?
scenarios.situation: A vendor claims their chain is 'fully decentralized.'
scenarios.title: Measuring decentralization
scenarios.why: Decentralization is multi-layered: consensus power, client development, governance, and infrastructure can each centralize independently. Node counts mislead when mining pools or validators concentrate. Engineers should ask: who can censor transactions? Who can change the rules? Who do I depend on? — per layer. The label is marketing; the power distribution is engineering.

choices: Accounts with balances, like a bank
UTXOs: unspent transaction outputs — each transaction consumes inputs and creates outputs; your 'balance' is the set of UTXOs you can spend
A single global balance sheet
It doesn't track ownership
scenarios.hint: When you 'send' bitcoin, what exactly are you consuming — and what are you creating?
scenarios.prompt: How does Bitcoin track ownership?
scenarios.situation: You're explaining to an Ethereum developer why Bitcoin has no accounts.
scenarios.title: Coins, not accounts
scenarios.why: Bitcoin's UTXO model: value lives in discrete unspent outputs, each locked to a spending condition. Transactions consume UTXOs as inputs and create new ones as outputs (with change returning to the sender). No account balances exist at the protocol level — wallets compute them by summing UTXOs. This shapes everything: privacy (new addresses per UTXO), validation, and fee estimation.

choices: To waste electricity
To make rewriting history prohibitively expensive: the longest-work chain wins, so altering a buried transaction requires redoing all subsequent work
To create new coins only
Miners enjoy puzzles
scenarios.hint: What would it cost to change a transaction six blocks deep?
scenarios.prompt: What security property does proof of work provide?
scenarios.situation: A skeptic calls PoW 'wasteful computation.'
scenarios.title: Work as security
scenarios.why: PoW converts energy into immutability: each block's work accumulates, so rewriting history means outpacing the honest network's ongoing work — economically infeasible for deep burials. The 'waste' critique misses the point: the cost IS the security. Whether that trade-off is worth it is a legitimate debate; what PoW buys is objective, verifiable, leaderless consensus.

choices: Blocks come whenever miners feel like it
Every 2016 blocks, difficulty retargets to maintain ~10-minute average block times despite changing hash power
Difficulty never changes
It's adjusted daily by developers
scenarios.hint: What keeps block times stable when hash power doubles overnight?
scenarios.prompt: How does Bitcoin keep block times stable?
scenarios.situation: Network hash rate doubled after a price rally.
scenarios.title: The retarget
scenarios.why: The difficulty retarget (every 2016 blocks, ~2 weeks) adjusts mining difficulty based on actual vs target block times, holding the ~10-minute average regardless of hash power. This is Bitcoin's monetary-policy engine room: stable block times mean predictable issuance. It's also why the network survived massive hash-rate shocks — the protocol adapts automatically, no committee required.

choices: Transactions confirm instantly
The lifecycle: creation → signing → broadcast → mempool → miner selection (fee market) → block inclusion → confirmations
Miners create transactions
The mempool is permanent storage
scenarios.hint: Where does a transaction wait — and who decides which waits end?
scenarios.prompt: What happens between clicking 'send' and confirmation?
scenarios.situation: A user's transaction is 'stuck' — unconfirmed for hours.
scenarios.title: Stuck in the mempool
scenarios.why: The mempool is the waiting room: unconfirmed transactions queue, and miners select by fee rate (satoshis per virtual byte) — it's a fee market, not a queue. 'Stuck' means underbid: the fix is fee bumping (RBF/CPFP), not resending. Understanding the lifecycle turns 'the network is broken' into 'the fee was too low' — and informs wallet fee-estimation design.

choices: SegWit was just a block-size increase
A protocol upgrade that fixed transaction malleability and separated witness data — enabling Layer 2 (Lightning) and changing fee economics
SegWit made Bitcoin centralized
It only affected miners
scenarios.hint: What did malleability break — and what does fixing it enable?
scenarios.prompt: Why did SegWit matter?
scenarios.situation: You're reviewing Bitcoin's upgrade history for protocol literacy.
scenarios.title: Segregating the witness
scenarios.why: SegWit fixed transaction malleability (third parties could alter txids before confirmation, breaking chains of unconfirmed transactions) by moving signatures out of the txid computation — which unblocked Layer 2 protocols like Lightning that depend on stable txids. It also introduced block weight, effectively raising capacity. Protocol upgrades are case studies in decentralized governance actually working.

choices: Lightning is a separate coin
A Layer 2 of payment channels: parties transact off-chain instantly and cheaply, settling net results on-chain — inheriting Bitcoin's security for the settlement
Lightning replaces Bitcoin
Channels require trusting a third party
scenarios.hint: What goes on-chain — every coffee purchase, or just the channel open and close?
scenarios.prompt: How does Lightning scale Bitcoin?
scenarios.situation: A merchant needs instant, low-fee Bitcoin payments.
scenarios.title: Off-chain, secured on-chain
scenarios.why: Lightning moves the volume off-chain: two parties lock funds in a channel, transact instantly via signed updates, and only the open/close (or disputes) touch the blockchain. Security comes from the ability to always settle on-chain — the chain is the court of final appeal. It's the layered-scaling thesis: base layer for settlement security, upper layers for speed and cost.

choices: Miners compete with proof of work
A consensus process among trusted validators: rounds of proposal and voting converge on the next ledger version every 3–5 seconds — no mining
A central server decides
It's proof of stake
scenarios.hint: If there's no mining, what do validators actually do every few seconds?
scenarios.prompt: How does the XRP Ledger reach agreement without mining?
scenarios.situation: You're comparing XRPL's consensus to Bitcoin's for an architecture review.
scenarios.title: Consensus without mining
scenarios.why: XRPL validators iteratively propose and vote on transaction sets until a supermajority agrees — converging on a validated ledger every 3–5 seconds. Security comes from validator overlap and the supermajority threshold, not energy expenditure. The trade-off: faster deterministic-ish close and low energy, versus Bitcoin's permissionless mining security model. Different trust assumptions, different design.

choices: XRP is just for speculation
XRP as a bridge currency and anti-spam mechanism: it enables cross-currency payments and each transaction destroys a tiny amount, making spam expensive
XRP has no protocol function
It's only for fees
scenarios.hint: What sits between two illiquid currencies in a payment path — and what stops someone from flooding the network?
scenarios.prompt: What is XRP's protocol-level function?
scenarios.situation: A payments engineer asks why XRP exists in the design.
scenarios.title: More than a token
scenarios.why: XRP serves two protocol functions: bridge currency (any currency can route through XRP for liquidity between otherwise illiquid pairs) and spam prevention (tiny destroyed fee per transaction makes flooding the ledger economically irrational). Understanding the native asset's mechanical role — not its price — is protocol literacy.

choices: Trust lines are just contacts
Trust lines: explicit on-ledger authorizations to hold an issuer's currency, with limits — the mechanism for issued currencies (stablecoins, etc.) on XRPL
Anyone can issue unlimited currency to anyone
Trust lines are off-chain
scenarios.hint: Why should the ledger let anyone force you to hold their IOU?
scenarios.prompt: How do non-XRP currencies work on the ledger?
scenarios.situation: A fintech wants to issue a USD stablecoin on XRPL.
scenarios.title: IOUs with consent
scenarios.why: Issued currencies on XRPL are IOUs: they only exist between an issuer and holders connected by trust lines — explicit, limited authorizations to hold that issuer's currency. No trust line, no balance. This elegantly models credit risk on-ledger: holding issued currency IS trusting the issuer, and the ledger records exactly who trusts whom, to what limit.

choices: Payments only work in XRP
Pathfinding: the ledger finds multi-hop paths across order books and trust lines to deliver the requested currency — auto-bridging through XRP or other currencies
You must hold every currency
Paths are manual
scenarios.hint: How does a payment in EUR reach someone who wants USD, with neither party touching the conversion?
scenarios.prompt: How do cross-currency payments work?
scenarios.situation: A user wants to pay USD to a recipient who wants EUR.
scenarios.title: Finding the path
scenarios.why: XRPL pathfinding computes routes through the ledger's liquidity graph — order books and trust lines — auto-bridging across currencies (often via XRP) so sender and recipient each deal in their own currency. The protocol does the FX. This is the payments-engine vision: currency-agnostic value transfer with the ledger as the exchange.

choices: Ledger close is probabilistic like Bitcoin
Validated ledgers close every 3–5 seconds with supermajority agreement — fast, regular settlement
Close times are random
Faster close means less security automatically
scenarios.hint: What does a 3–5 second rhythm buy a payments use case — and what does it assume?
scenarios.prompt: What does the 3–5 second ledger close mean practically?
scenarios.situation: You're sizing XRPL for a remittance product.
scenarios.title: Seconds, not minutes
scenarios.why: A validated ledger every 3–5 seconds means payment finality on a human-interaction timescale — the remittance use case actually works. The speed comes from the validator-voting consensus rather than PoW's probabilistic race. The engineering question is always the trade: what trust assumption buys this speed, and does your use case accept it?

choices: XRPL has no smart contracts at all
The ledger prioritizes native transaction types and robustness over general programmability — a deliberate design trade differing from EVM-style chains
It's less advanced
Native types are a limitation with no benefit
scenarios.hint: What bugs are impossible when the transaction types are fixed and native?
scenarios.prompt: How does XRPL's design philosophy differ from EVM chains?
scenarios.situation: A Solidity developer asks why XRPL 'lacks' smart contracts.
scenarios.title: Native vs programmable
scenarios.why: XRPL's philosophy: implement core financial operations (payments, DEX, escrow, channels) as native, reviewed transaction types rather than user smart contracts. The trade: less general programmability, but the most-exploited contract bug classes simply can't exist in native code paths. It's a different point on the flexibility-safety spectrum — understand the trade before judging the design.

choices: The EVM is just a slow computer
A deterministic stack-based virtual machine: every node executes the same bytecode and reaches the same state — the foundation of smart-contract trustlessness
It's only for Solidity
Gas is optional
scenarios.hint: Why must execution be deterministic — what breaks if two nodes compute different results?
scenarios.prompt: What is the EVM's execution model, and why deterministic?
scenarios.situation: You're explaining smart contracts to a traditional backend engineer.
scenarios.title: The world computer's rules
scenarios.why: The EVM is a deterministic state machine: given the same state and transaction, every node computes the identical result — that's what lets mutually distrusting nodes agree on contract outcomes. Determinism forbids randomness, wall-clock time, and external calls inside execution; oracles and commit-reveal exist precisely because of this constraint. The determinism IS the trust model.

choices: Gas is just a fee
Gas meters computation: every operation costs gas, bounding execution (halting problem solved economically) and pricing block space — out-of-gas reverts state changes
Gas is refunded always
Unlimited loops are fine
scenarios.hint: What stops an infinite loop on a blockchain — and who pays for the attempt?
scenarios.prompt: What problem does gas solve?
scenarios.situation: A developer's contract keeps running out of gas.
scenarios.title: Paying for computation
scenarios.why: Gas solves the halting problem economically: computation must terminate because the sender's gas runs out, and every operation's price reflects its cost to the network. Out-of-gas reverts state (but consumes the gas — the work was done). For developers, gas shapes design: storage is brutally expensive, loops over unbounded arrays are bugs, and 'gas golfing' is real engineering.

choices: They're the same — both store data
Storage persists on-chain across transactions (expensive, ~20k gas per slot); memory is transient per-call (cheap). Choosing wrong wastes enormous gas or loses data
Always use storage — it's safer
Memory persists between calls
scenarios.hint: What happens to memory when the call ends — and what does a storage write cost?
scenarios.prompt: When do you use storage vs memory?
scenarios.situation: A contract stores loop temporaries in storage and costs a fortune.
scenarios.title: Storage is the expensive one
scenarios.why: EVM storage (SSTORE) writes to permanent chain state — ~20,000 gas per new slot, the most expensive common operation. Memory is per-call scratch space, cheap and discarded. The bug pattern: using storage for temporaries, or reading storage repeatedly in loops instead of caching to memory. Gas-aware Solidity starts with knowing where each variable lives.

choices: Events are just logs for debugging
Events: cheap append-only logs (bloom-filter indexed) for off-chain consumption — the contract-to-world communication channel; they don't affect state
Events can change state
Off-chain apps should poll storage instead
scenarios.hint: How does a frontend learn a transfer happened — by re-reading all state, or by listening?
scenarios.prompt: What are events for?
scenarios.situation: A dApp frontend needs to track token transfers in real time.
scenarios.title: The contract speaks
scenarios.why: Events are the EVM's cheap broadcast mechanism: contracts emit them, off-chain indexers and frontends subscribe — no polling, no state reads. They're orders of magnitude cheaper than storage and bloom-indexed for efficient filtering. But they're write-only from the chain's perspective: contracts can't read their own events. Design the off-chain architecture around events from day one.

choices: Contracts call each other like normal functions — no special risk
External calls hand control to untrusted code: the called contract can reenter before state updates — the reentrancy class. Update state BEFORE external calls (checks-effects-interactions)
Reentrancy is theoretical
Only call trusted contracts
scenarios.hint: What happens if msg.sender is a contract whose fallback calls withdraw() again — before balances is zeroed?
scenarios.prompt: What is the vulnerability?
scenarios.situation: An audit flags this withdrawal function.
scenarios.title: The DAO's lesson
scenarios.why: The external call happens BEFORE the balance is zeroed — a malicious recipient contract reenters withdraw() and drains funds repeatedly. This exact pattern caused The DAO hack. The fix pattern (checks-effects-interactions): update state first, then interact. Every external call is a trust boundary; the EVM will happily call attacker code mid-function.

choices: Contracts are immutable — deal with it
Upgradeability is a deliberate trade: proxy patterns enable fixes but reintroduce trust (who controls the upgrade?) — choose explicitly and disclose it
Upgrades are always safe
Immutable contracts need no audits
scenarios.hint: What does 'immutable' protect — and what does it cost when there's a bug?
scenarios.prompt: How should teams think about upgradeable contracts?
scenarios.situation: The team debates proxy-upgradeable vs immutable deployment.
scenarios.title: To upgrade or not
scenarios.why: Immutability is a security property (users know the rules can't change) and an operational risk (bugs are forever). Proxy patterns buy fixability at the cost of reintroducing trusted upgrade authority — which must itself be governed (multisig, timelock). There's no universally right answer; there's only the explicit trade-off, disclosed to users. 'Upgradeable' without governance is just centralized control.

choices: Only the contract's own functions matter
Every external call, oracle input, and privileged role is a trust boundary — map them explicitly and minimize trust at each
Trust boundaries don't apply on-chain
Only the admin is a boundary
scenarios.hint: Where does untrusted input or control enter your contract?
scenarios.prompt: How do you threat-model a smart contract?
scenarios.situation: You're reviewing a DeFi contract before audit.
scenarios.title: Mapping the boundaries
scenarios.why: Contract threat modeling enumerates trust boundaries: external calls (untrusted code execution), oracle feeds (who controls the data?), privileged roles (who can rug?), and economic assumptions (what breaks if prices move?). Each boundary gets a control: reentrancy guards, oracle validation, timelocks, circuit breakers. Unmapped boundaries are where the exploits live.

choices: Ownable is enough for everything
Role-based access control: least-privilege roles, timelocked admin actions, and ideally multisig for critical functions — single-key admin is a centralization risk
Access control doesn't matter on-chain
Give everyone admin
scenarios.hint: What happens when the single admin key is compromised — or the admin turns malicious?
scenarios.prompt: What is proper access control for a protocol contract?
scenarios.situation: The contract has a single owner with sweeping powers and no timelock.
scenarios.title: The god key
scenarios.why: A single EOA admin is a single point of failure AND a rug vector: compromise or malice drains the protocol. Mature designs use role-based permissions (minting ≠ upgrading ≠ pausing), timelocks on sensitive actions (users can exit before changes), and multisig control. 'Decentralized protocol, centralized admin' is the contradiction auditors flag first.

choices: Oracles are trusted by definition
Oracle risk: contracts consuming off-chain data inherit the oracle's trust assumptions — validate feeds (multiple sources, deviation checks, staleness guards, circuit breakers)
Use one oracle — simpler
Oracle data can't be manipulated
scenarios.hint: What is the contract actually trusting — the data, or the mechanism that delivered it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle price-feed risk?
scenarios.situation: A lending contract liquidates based on a single DEX spot price.
scenarios.title: The oracle problem
scenarios.why: A single-source spot price is manipulable (flash-loan attacks have drained protocols exactly this way). Defense in depth: multiple independent sources, time-weighted averages, deviation circuit breakers, and staleness checks. The contract's security is bounded by its weakest oracle — 'the price feed said so' is not a defense when the feed was the attack vector.

choices: Front-running is impossible on-chain
Ordering risk: public mempools let searchers see and outbid your transaction — design with commit-reveal, batch auctions, or MEV-aware mechanisms where ordering matters
It's only a miner problem
Users don't need to know
scenarios.hint: Who sees your transaction before it's confirmed — and what can they do with that preview?
scenarios.prompt: What is the front-running/MEV risk for your DEX?
scenarios.situation: Users complain their trades execute at worse prices than quoted.
scenarios.title: The invisible tax
scenarios.why: Public mempools are an all-see preview: searchers sandwich user trades (buy before, sell after) or outbid liquidations. It's a structural property of transparent ordering, not a bug in your contract — but your design must account for it: slippage limits protect users partially; commit-reveal or batch auctions change the game. Ignoring MEV means your users pay it.

choices: Audits guarantee security

Audits are expert review, not proof: scope them tightly, fix findings, re-audit fixes, and layer defenses (bounties, monitoring, circuit breakers, upgrade governance) — defense in depth past the audit

scenarios.title: Beyond the audit

choices: It's a cryptocurrency

It's not a coin; it's infrastructure for consortia that need governance, not anonymity.

choices: Channels are just chat rooms

scenarios.situation: You're porting a business process to Fabric.
scenarios.title: Code with endorsers
scenarios.why: Chaincode encodes the business rules, but Fabric's distinctive mechanism is endorsement: transactions must be endorsed (simulated and signed) by specified peers per policy BEFORE ordering and commitment. choices: Miners order transactions

Ordering is done by clients
Order doesn't matter

scenarios.prompt: What does the ordering service do, and why is it separate?
scenarios.situation: You're explaining Fabric's architecture to a Fabric-newcomer.
scenarios.title: Ordering the chaos
scenarios.why: Fabric separates execution (endorsement) from ordering (sequencing) from validation (commit) — the ordering service establishes the single canonical transaction order all peers then validate and commit deterministically. Order is consensus; execution is endorsement.

choices: Participants are anonymous

Identity doesn't matter
It's username/password

scenarios.situation: Compliance requires knowing exactly who did what on the network.
scenarios.title: Known participants

Enterprise should always use public chains
Throughput is the only criterion

scenarios.prompt: How do you choose between Hyperledger-style and public-chain approaches?
scenarios.situation: A supply-chain consortium is choosing its platform.
scenarios.title: Fitting the platform
scenarios.why: The decision rests on trust reality: known, contracted participants with confidentiality needs and governance requirements fit permissioned frameworks; open participation with censorship resistance needs fits permissionless. Supply-chain consortia (known partners, competitive data, throughput needs) typically land permissioned. Platform choice follows the trust model — not the hype cycle.

scenarios.title: Scoping the Capstone
scenarios.situation: You want to build a full-stack dApp with smart contracts and web3 frontend for your portfolio. You have 4 weeks of evenings. You're tempted to add every feature you've learned.

Include every topic from the bootcamp — comprehensive coverage impresses employers most
Build the most technically impressive version — complexity demonstrates advanced skills
Skip planning and start building — you'll figure out scope as you go
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A finished MVP proves competence; an unfinished ambitious project proves nothing. Employers value completed work with clear decisions. scenarios.title: When You're Stuck
scenarios.situation: Week 2 of your full-stack dApp with smart contracts and web3 frontend. You've hit a technical blocker — a key integration isn't working and documentation is unclear. You've spent 3 evenings on it.
scenarios.prompt: What's the most productive approach?
choices: Timebox 2 more hours, then pivot: document the blocker, implement a workaround or simplified version, and note it as a known limitation with future improvement plans
Keep pushing until it works — giving up on a technical challenge shows weakness
Abandon the current approach and rewrite everything using a different technology
Skip that feature entirely and pretend it was never planned
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Professional engineers timebox investigations and pivot strategically. Documenting the blocker and implementing a workaround shows problem-solving maturity. Endless grinding wastes capstone time. Rewriting introduces new risks. Pretending the feature was never planned is dishonest and loses a learning opportunity.
scenarios.hint: How do professional engineers handle blockers under deadline? What demonstrates maturity?

scenarios.title: Pre-Submission Review
scenarios.situation: Your full-stack dApp with smart contracts and web3 frontend is functionally complete. You have 3 days before you want to publish it to your portfolio.
scenarios.prompt: What's the highest-value use of the remaining time?
choices: Polish and verify: test the demo end-to-end, proofread documentation, verify the README renders correctly, record a backup demo video, and do a final security/best-practices review
Add 2-3 more features to make it more impressive
Rewrite the code to be more elegant — first drafts are always messy
Publish immediately — done is better than perfect
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A polished, working project with great documentation beats a feature-rich buggy one. Demo failures during interviews are catastrophic. README quality signals professionalism. A backup video saves you if live demo fails. Adding features now risks breaking working code. Publishing without review risks embarrassing errors.
scenarios.hint: What causes the most damage in a portfolio review: missing features or broken demos?
evidence: Demo works | README complete | Video recorded | Security reviewed

scenarios.title: Defending Your Capstone

Explain that you followed best practices from your bootcamp
Focus on the code — offer to walk through the implementation line by line

lessons.title: Blockchain Basics — Core concepts
concepts: Distributed ledger: consensus is the mechanism by which decentralized participants converge on one ledger state — ordering transactions and resolving conflicts without a trusted coordinator.

Trust model: the models encode different trust assumptions: permissionless assumes adversarial anonymity (secured by economic incentives), permissioned assumes known identities with contractual/legal accountability.

Consensus: different mechanisms (PoW, PoS, XRPL consensus) make different trade-offs, but the problem they solve is identical: agreement among adversaries. Decentralization is multi-layered: consensus power, client development, governance, and infrastructure can each centralize independently.
Permissioned vs permissionless: inter-bank settlement among regulated entities fits permissioned — identity, privacy, and governance matter more than censorship resistance.

Trust assumptions: blockchain's benefits (trust minimization, tamper-evidence across distrusting parties) come at real costs: throughput limits, complexity, immutability conflicts with data-deletion requirements.

lessons.title: Bitcoin Protocol — Core concepts
concepts: UTXO model: bitcoin's UTXO model: value lives in discrete unspent outputs, each locked to a spending condition.

Transaction structure: segWit fixed transaction malleability (third parties could alter txids before confirmation, breaking chains of unconfirmed transactions) by moving signatures out of the txid computation — which unblocked Layer 2 protocols like Lightning that depend on stable txids.
Proof of work: poW converts energy into immutability: each block's work accumulates, so rewriting history means outpacing the honest network's ongoing work — economically infeasible for deep burials.
Security model: it's the layered-scaling thesis: base layer for settlement security, upper layers for speed and cost.
Difficulty adjustment: the difficulty retarget (every 2016 blocks, ~2 weeks) adjusts mining difficulty based on actual vs target block times, holding the ~10-minute average regardless of hash power.

lessons.title: XRPL — Core concepts
concepts: XRPL pathfinding computes routes through the ledger's liquidity graph — order books and trust lines — auto-bridging across currencies (often via XRP) so sender and recipient each deal in their own currency.
Validator voting: security comes from validator overlap and the supermajority threshold, not energy expenditure.

XRP serves two protocol functions: bridge currency (any currency can route through XRP for liquidity between otherwise illiquid pairs) and spam prevention (tiny destroyed fee per transaction makes flooding the ledger economically irrational).
Bridge currency: this elegantly models credit risk on-ledger: holding issued currency IS trusting the issuer, and the ledger records exactly who trusts whom, to what limit.
Trust lines: the engineering question is always the trade: what trust assumption buys this speed, and does your use case accept it? Different trust assumptions, different design.

lessons.title: Solidity & EVM — Core concepts
concepts: EVM storage (SSTORE) writes to permanent chain state — ~20,000 gas per new slot, the most expensive common operation. Events are the EVM's cheap broadcast mechanism: contracts emit them, off-chain indexers and frontends subscribe — no polling, no state reads.

Deterministic execution: the EVM is a deterministic state machine: given the same state and transaction, every node computes the identical result — that's what lets mutually distrusting nodes agree on contract outcomes.

Gas: for developers, gas shapes design: storage is brutally expensive, loops over unbounded arrays are bugs, and 'gas golfing' is real engineering. Gas-aware Solidity starts with knowing where each variable lives.
Execution bounds: determinism forbids randomness, wall-clock time, and external calls inside execution; oracles and commit-reveal exist precisely because of this constraint.
Storage vs memory: memory is per-call scratch space, cheap and discarded. They're orders of magnitude cheaper than storage and bloom-indexed for efficient filtering.
Gas solves the halting problem economically: computation must terminate because the sender's gas runs out, and every operation's price reflects its cost to the network.

concepts: Trust boundaries: contract threat modeling enumerates trust boundaries: external calls (untrusted code execution), oracle feeds (who controls the data?), privileged roles (who can rug?), and economic assumptions (what breaks if prices move?).
Threat modeling: happy-path unit tests verify intent; adversarial testing (property-based fuzzing, fork tests, economic modeling) verifies robustness.
Access control: each boundary gets a control: reentrancy guards, oracle validation, timelocks, circuit breakers.

Admin risk: a single EOA admin is a single point of failure AND a rug vector: compromise or malice drains the protocol. An audit is a point-in-time expert review of scoped code — it reduces risk, it doesn't eliminate it.
Oracle risk: the contract's security is bounded by its weakest oracle — 'the price feed said so' is not a defense when the feed was the attack vector.

lessons.title: Hyperledger Concepts — Core concepts
concepts: Hyperledger is a Linux Foundation greenhouse of enterprise blockchain frameworks — permissioned networks, known identities, modular consensus, private transactions.

Enterprise blockchain: the enterprise requirements (who's on the network, who sees what data, how many TPS) drive fundamentally different designs than permissionless chains. For regulated consortia, it's the feature that makes blockchain deployable.
Channels partition the ledger: each channel has its own ledger, members, and chaincode — participants only see channels they belong to.

Data isolation: channel design IS the data-governance architecture; getting it wrong leaks competitively sensitive data to the consortium. Supply-chain consortia (known partners, competitive data, throughput needs) typically land permissioned.

Chaincode encodes the business rules, but Fabric's distinctive mechanism is endorsement: transactions must be endorsed (simulated and signed) by specified peers per policy BEFORE ordering and commitment.

Endorsement: fabric separates execution (endorsement) from ordering (sequencing) from validation (commit) — the ordering service establishes the single canonical transaction order all peers then validate and commit deterministically.

lessons.title: Blockchain Development — Core concepts
concepts: A blockchain is an append-only ledger replicated across nodes; consensus is the protocol by which mutually distrusting nodes agree on the next block — proof-of-work (energy, probabilistic finality), proof-of-stake (economic stake, finalized epochs), and federated agreement like Stellar's SCP (quorum slices, seconds-fast close).

The EVM executes deterministic bytecode where every operation costs gas: the gas limit buys computation and the gas price buys inclusion priority. Out-of-gas reverts state changes but the spent gas is still paid.

Smart contracts are public programs: any external function is callable by anyone, so authorization must be enforced on-chain (require checks on msg.sender). Ordering matters — update state before external calls (checks-effects-interactions) to close reentrancy.
Wallets hold keys, not coins: a BIP39 mnemonic derives every account via BIP32/BIP44 paths. Possession of the seed equals possession of all funds — it must never be stored digitally or shared.

Ledger designs trade transparency for privacy: Bitcoin's UTXO model is transparent and analyzable, while Monero combines ring signatures, stealth addresses, and confidential amounts for privacy by default — at the cost of larger transactions.

Real-world value rails use messaging standards too: ISO 20022's structured MX messages (e.g., pacs.008) carry machine-readable payment data that legacy free-text formats cannot, which is why migrations must map data models, not just fields.

example.walkthrough: The deployer becomes owner; deposit() credits an internal ledger. withdraw() follows checks-effects-interactions: it validates, reduces the balance first, and only then makes the external call — so a malicious recipient that re-enters finds nothing left to drain. Add an onlyOwner function and a reentrancy guard before this pattern touches real value.

pitfalls: Common trap: testing only on a local chain and reusing a transfer-sized gas limit on mainnet — estimate gas for the real call path.
Common trap: treating testnet tokens or screenshots of a seed phrase as harmless — testnet habits become mainnet habits.
Common trap: hiding a privileged function from the UI instead of restricting it on-chain — attackers call contracts directly.
Common trap: confusing confirmations with finality — unfinalized blocks can reorganize; match the guarantee to the value at risk.

simulations.brief: A transaction you broadcast is stuck unconfirmed for hours. Diagnose it.
simulations.debrief: Stuck transactions are almost always fee problems. Replace-by-fee or child-pays-for-parent unsticks them — resending the same fee changes nothing.

evidence: Your tx: 1 sat/vB. Mempool minimum for next block: 25 sat/vB.
steps.explain: At 1 sat/vB against a 25 sat/vB market, miners will not pick it up. The fee is the problem, not the network.
options: The fee is far below market — bump it with replace-by-fee
The network is broken; wait indefinitely

evidence: Transaction was broadcast with RBF enabled (sequence < max).
steps.explain: RBF signaling means you can replace the transaction with a higher-fee version. Without RBF, child-pays-for-parent is the fallback.
options: Use replace-by-fee to broadcast a higher-fee replacement
Ask miners nicely on social media
steps.symptom: RBF was enabled. What is the fix?

evidence: Replacement confirmed in the next block.
steps.explain: The replacement confirmed because it paid the market rate. Fee estimation before broadcast prevents the whole episode.
options: Check fee estimates before broadcasting next time
Use the same fee out of habit
steps.symptom: Confirmed. What is the lasting lesson?

sections.heading: Blockchain Basics
items: Distributed ledger — consensus is the mechanism by which decentralized participants converge on one ledger state — ordering transactions and resolving conflicts without a trusted coordinator.

Trust model — the models encode different trust assumptions: permissionless assumes adversarial anonymity (secured by economic incentives), permissioned assumes known identities with contractual/legal accountability.

Consensus — different mechanisms (PoW, PoS, XRPL consensus) make different trade-offs, but the problem they solve is identical: agreement among adversaries. Decentralization is multi-layered: consensus power, client development, governance, and infrastructure can each…
Permissioned vs permissionless — inter-bank settlement among regulated entities fits permissioned — identity, privacy, and governance matter more than censorship resistance.

Trust assumptions — blockchain's benefits (trust minimization, tamper-evidence across distrusting parties) come at real costs: throughput limits, complexity, immutability conflicts with data-deletion requirements.
Common trap — decentralization means no one is in charge of anything.
Common trap — finality means the transaction is fast.
Common trap — finality doesn't matter for applications.

sections.heading: Bitcoin Protocol
items: UTXO model — bitcoin's UTXO model: value lives in discrete unspent outputs, each locked to a spending condition.

Transaction structure — segWit fixed transaction malleability (third parties could alter txids before confirmation, breaking chains of unconfirmed transactions) by moving signatures out of the txid computation — which unblocked Layer 2 protocols like Lightning that depend on stabl…

Proof of work — poW converts energy into immutability: each block's work accumulates, so rewriting history means outpacing the honest network's ongoing work — economically infeasible for deep burials.
Security model — it's the layered-scaling thesis: base layer for settlement security, upper layers for speed and cost.
Difficulty adjustment — the difficulty retarget (every 2016 blocks, ~2 weeks) adjusts mining difficulty based on actual vs target block times, holding the ~10-minute average regardless of hash power.
Common trap — segWit made Bitcoin centralized.
Common trap — blocks come whenever miners feel like it.
Common trap — channels require trusting a third party.
Common trap — accounts with balances, like a bank.

sections.heading: XRPL
items: XRPL pathfinding computes routes through the ledger's liquidity graph — order books and trust lines — auto-bridging across currencies (often via XRP) so sender and recipient each deal in their own currency.
Validator voting — security comes from validator overlap and the supermajority threshold, not energy expenditure.

XRP serves two protocol functions — bridge currency (any currency can route through XRP for liquidity between otherwise illiquid pairs) and spam prevention (tiny destroyed fee per transaction makes flooding the ledger economically irrational).
Bridge currency — this elegantly models credit risk on-ledger: holding issued currency IS trusting the issuer, and the ledger records exactly who trusts whom, to what limit.
Trust lines — the engineering question is always the trade: what trust assumption buys this speed, and does your use case accept it? Different trust assumptions, different design.
Common trap — validated ledgers close every 3–5 seconds with supermajority agreement.
Common trap — faster close means less security automatically.
Common trap — anyone can issue unlimited currency to anyone.

items: EVM storage (SSTORE) writes to permanent chain state — ~20,000 gas per new slot, the most expensive common operation. Events are the EVM's cheap broadcast mechanism: contracts emit them, off-chain indexers and frontends subscribe — no polling, no state reads.

Deterministic execution — the EVM is a deterministic state machine: given the same state and transaction, every node computes the identical result — that's what lets mutually distrusting nodes agree on contract outcomes.

Gas — for developers, gas shapes design: storage is brutally expensive, loops over unbounded arrays are bugs, and 'gas golfing' is real engineering. Gas-aware Solidity starts with knowing where each variable lives.
Execution bounds — determinism forbids randomness, wall-clock time, and external calls inside execution; oracles and commit-reveal exist precisely because of this constraint.
Storage vs memory — memory is per-call scratch space, cheap and discarded. They're orders of magnitude cheaper than storage and bloom-indexed for efficient filtering.
Gas solves the halting problem economically — computation must terminate because the sender's gas runs out, and every operation's price reflects its cost to the network.
Common trap — off-chain apps should poll storage instead.
Common trap — contracts call each other like normal functions.
Common trap — immutable contracts need no audits.

sections.heading: Security
items: Trust boundaries — contract threat modeling enumerates trust boundaries: external calls (untrusted code execution), oracle feeds (who controls the data?), privileged roles (who can rug?), and economic assumptions (what breaks if prices move?).
Threat modeling — happy-path unit tests verify intent; adversarial testing (property-based fuzzing, fork tests, economic modeling) verifies robustness.
Access control — each boundary gets a control: reentrancy guards, oracle validation, timelocks, circuit breakers.

Admin risk — a single EOA admin is a single point of failure AND a rug vector: compromise or malice drains the protocol. An audit is a point-in-time expert review of scoped code — it reduces risk, it doesn't eliminate it.
Oracle risk — the contract's security is bounded by its weakest oracle — 'the price feed said so' is not a defense when the feed was the attack vector.
Common trap — access control doesn't matter on-chain.
Common trap — trust boundaries don't apply on-chain.
Common trap — formal verification is unnecessary overhead to even consider.
Common trap — one audit is enough forever.

sections.heading: Hyperledger Concepts
items: Hyperledger — is a Linux Foundation greenhouse of enterprise blockchain frameworks — permissioned networks, known identities, modular consensus, private transactions.

Enterprise blockchain — the enterprise requirements (who's on the network, who sees what data, how many TPS) drive fundamentally different designs than permissionless chains. For regulated consortia, it's the feature that makes blockchain deployable.
Channels partition the ledger — each channel has its own ledger, members, and chaincode — participants only see channels they belong to.

Data isolation — channel design IS the data-governance architecture; getting it wrong leaks competitively sensitive data to the consortium. Supply-chain consortia (known partners, competitive data, throughput needs) typically land permissioned.

Chaincode — Chaincode encodes the business rules, but Fabric's distinctive mechanism is endorsement: transactions must be endorsed (simulated and signed) by specified peers per policy BEFORE ordering and commitment.

Endorsement — fabric separates execution (endorsement) from ordering (sequencing) from validation (commit) — the ordering service establishes the single canonical transaction order all peers then validate and commit deterministically.
Common trap — chaincode is just a smart contract by another name.
Common trap — enterprise should always use public chains.
Common trap — permissioned means less secure.
